verdicts.text: In both Pulumi ESC and HashiCorp Vault, secrets can be stored and accessed through a CLI, SDK, or editor interface.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs describe a Vault CLI and a Vault UI, both built on the HTTP API ("both the CLI and UI internally rely on these same API calls"), plus officially maintained client libraries ("These libraries are officially maintained by HashiCorp"). So Vault has all three access methods, with its web UI counting as the 'editor interface'. The ESC half (esc CLI, esc-sdk, and the Pulumi Cloud environment editor) is Pulumi's own product and was not checked against product source in this lane.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim calls it an 'editor interface'. For Vault, that maps to the web UI, where you can create and edit secrets.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is fully open source and licensed under Apache 2.0.
verdicts.evidence: The GitHub API shows pulumi/esc (the CLI and evaluation engine) is licensed "Apache-2.0", so the license itself is correct. But ESC runs as a service on Pulumi Cloud, which is not open source, and the same page (L52) calls it a "Fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud". So "fully open source" claims more than the Apache-licensed repo covers.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc --jq .license.spdx_id → Apache-2.0; repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L52
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the source shows 'the pulumi/esc repo (CLI/engine) is Apache-2.0'; the claim says 'Pulumi ESC is fully open source', which leaves out that the hosted Pulumi Cloud service is proprietary
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Fully open source" is a strong thing to say about a product sold as SaaS on Pulumi Cloud.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC provides composability of collections of secrets and configuration, allowing environments to be composed together from multiple other environments so that shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Each environment can be composed from multiple environments." It also says: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration." The local ESC docs index backs this up with its "Compose environments — Import environments to share configuration across teams" card.

verdicts.text: Through Pulumi ESC, secrets referenced from HashiCorp Vault can be organized as collections that are versioned, branched, and composed inside other collections.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The pulumi/esc README supports the "versioned" and "composed" parts: "Each environment can be composed from multiple environments" and "Every environment can be locked down with RBAC, versioned, and audited." I found no independent source for "branched." Only Pulumi docs pages use that word, including the live copy of the page under review, and those can't verify this claim.
verdicts.source: https://github.com/pulumi/esc (README); WebSearch ran query "Pulumi ESC vs HashiCorp Vault environments versioned composed"
verdicts.intuition_flag: ESC has revisions, version tags, and a clone feature, but as far as I know no Git-style branching of environments. "Branched" may be marketing wording the product doesn't back up.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is licensed under the Apache License 2.0, while HashiCorp Vault is licensed under the Business Source License 1.1.
verdicts.evidence: GitHub's license API reports pulumi/esc as "Apache License 2.0" (spdx Apache-2.0). The hashicorp/vault LICENSE file (base64-decoded) says "Licensed Work: Vault Version 1.15.0 or later" and "Business Source License 1.1", with MPL 2.0 as the change license.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc (license field); gh api repos/hashicorp/vault/contents/LICENSE
verdicts.framing_note: Caveats: Apache 2.0 covers the open-source pulumi/esc repo (the CLI and evaluation engine), not the hosted Pulumi Cloud ESC service. BSL applies to Vault 1.15.0 and later; older versions were MPL 2.0.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault offers a hosted cloud service and self-hosting, and self-hosting requires significant management overhead.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's own docs say "HCP Vault Dedicated is a hosted version of Vault Enterprise operated by Hashicorp on your behalf." Self-hosted Vault is still offered (Community Edition and Enterprise). HashiCorp describes self-managed Vault as requiring you to maintain "multiple regional clusters, infrastructure, monitoring systems, and on-call staffing", which supports the overhead point.
verdicts.framing_note: "Significant management overhead" is a qualitative judgment. HashiCorp's own material and third-party sources support it ("requires significant operational investment").
verdicts.intuition_flag: HCP Vault Secrets, the lighter SaaS option, shut down by July 1, 2026. Only HCP Vault Dedicated is still hosted, so the doc should not suggest a lightweight SaaS tier.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault supports a key-value store.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's official Vault docs say: "The kv secrets engine is a generic key-value store used to store arbitrary secrets within the configured physical storage for Vault."
verdicts.framing_note: The docs call it "a generic key-value store"; the claim says Vault "supports a key-value store". Same assertion.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault offers a limited key/value form editor with a JSON toggle for editing and authoring.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's own KV v2 tutorial describes the UI's key/value form with a JSON toggle: "Notice the JSON toggle in the UI. Instead of entering the key-value pairs one by one, you can enter the secret values using JSON." A GitHub feature request (#6909) says the JSON view is just a plain text box. That supports the word "limited", but "limited" is an opinion, not something a source can confirm.
verdicts.framing_note: Nobody disputes that the form editor and JSON toggle exist. "Limited" is the author's own judgment; the 2019 feature request (#6909) backs it up, but that request may be out of date.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC's CLI, available as `pulumi env` in the Pulumi CLI, supports injecting application secrets as environment variables and modifying secrets.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference lists the `pulumi env` subcommands, including `run`, `set`, `edit` and `remove`. For `pulumi env run` it says: "each key-value pair in the object is made available to the command as an environment variable". `pulumi env set` is described as "Set a value within an environment."

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault Agent's process supervisor mode covers injecting secrets as environment variables separately from the `vault` CLI.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp docs confirm env-var injection goes through Vault Agent's process supervisor mode: "Vault Agent's Process Supervisor Mode allows Vault secrets to be injected into a process via environment variables." It's configured with env_template and exec blocks in the Agent config, not through plain vault CLI commands. One caveat: Agent itself runs as the `vault agent` subcommand of the same binary.
verdicts.framing_note: Docs describe env-var injection as an Agent feature that needs its own config (env_template plus exec blocks), which fits the claim that it is handled separately from the CLI.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports a declarative provider via the Pulumi Service Provider, which allows management (create, update, delete) of collections of secrets and configuration as a resource through infrastructure as code.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/pulumi-pulumiservice provider ships an Environment resource (provider/pkg/resources/environment.go, with environment_version_tag.go and team_environment_perm.go next to it). That means ESC environments, which are collections of secrets and configuration, can be managed as IaC resources through the Pulumi Service Provider.
verdicts.framing_note: I only confirmed that environment.go exists and didn't read its code. The create/update/delete support is inferred from standard provider resource behavior.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports composability through hierarchical environments that inherit values from the environments they import.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC imports concepts page says: "Pulumi ESC allows you to compose environments by importing configuration and secrets from other environments... and enables you to organize configuration hierarchically." It also says imported values "are merged into the current environment using a JSON Merge Patch, with the current values overwriting the imported environment's values", which is inheritance with local overrides.
verdicts.framing_note: The evidence is a separate Pulumi docs page, not product source. I couldn't check the pulumi/esc source because the GitHub API hit its rate limit.

verdicts.text: In HashiCorp Vault, values can only be secrets.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's KV docs describe every stored value as a secret: "The kv secrets engine is used to store arbitrary secrets within the configured physical storage for Vault." They also say "only the values set on keys are" encrypted. Vault has no separate type for plaintext, non-secret config values the way ESC does. Vault will still accept any data you write, though, so this is a reasonable reading of the docs rather than a hard limit stated anywhere.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim cites no source. Vault's docs treat every KV value as a secret, but they never say non-secret values are forbidden.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Can only be secrets" is a comparison-page simplification: Vault will store non-sensitive data too, it just treats and encrypts everything as a secret.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault does not provide the ability to see existing secrets.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's official CLI docs say Vault lets you list and read the secrets it stores: "The 'kv list' command lists data from Vault's KV secrets engine at the given path." The `read` command page adds that it "can be used to read secrets, generate dynamic credentials, get configuration details."
verdicts.intuition_flag: A comparison-table row may have meant something narrower (e.g., seeing secrets that live in external or third-party stores, or seeing values across environments). As written, though, the sentence denies a core Vault feature. The author should say what the row actually compares.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports secret referencing: environments can import secrets from another environment, and secrets updated in the referenced environment automatically propagate to downstream environments.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration." Imports are resolved each time an environment is opened, so a change to the imported environment shows up downstream. I didn't fetch a passage that says "propagate" in those words, though.
verdicts.framing_note: Imports that pin a version (env@tag or env@revision, mentioned in the page's Versioning row) won't pick up upstream changes automatically. "Automatically propagate" holds only for imports that aren't pinned.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault has no equivalent concept to secret referencing; Vault has no first-class environment to reference, so secrets are read by path.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Vault's KV engine "allows you to store arbitrary key-value pairs at specified paths," and clients read secrets by path. A HashiCorp Discuss thread asking whether one KV secret can reference another ("I want to reference the secret app1.db.password") suggests there is no native feature for this. No Vault doc says outright that Vault has no referencing or environment concept, so this negative claim rests on circumstantial evidence.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is an absolute negative claim ("no equivalent concept"). Vault Agent/consul-template templating can combine several secret paths, which some readers might count as referencing.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC allows new dynamic values to be constructed through string interpolation of other values.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC evaluator source has an `Interpolation` AST type, and `parseInterpolate` parses `${...}` property accesses inside string values, with `$$` as the escape. That means ESC can build new values by interpolating other values into strings.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be forked for testing (branching) without rewriting entire environments and overriding specific values.
verdicts.evidence: ESC has no feature literally called "fork", but it supports both ways the claim describes. You can copy an environment with `pulumi env clone`, whose auto-generated CLI reference says it will "Clone an existing environment into a new environment." You can also import an environment and override only some values, since imported values "are merged into the current environment using a JSON Merge Patch, with the current values overwriting the imported environment's values where keys are redefined."
verdicts.intuition_flag: The docs call this "forking", but ESC has no fork command, only clone and import-plus-override. The sentence is also awkward: "without rewriting entire environments and overriding specific values" could be read as saying you don't override values at all.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault does not support branching or personal configs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) No HashiCorp source mentions a native branching feature for secrets/config. KV v2 only offers linear versioning, which fits the "no branching" half. The "no personal configs" half is disputable: Vault's own policy docs show a templated policy that "creates a section of the KVv2 Secret Engine to a specific user", which gives per-user secret space through policy templating.
verdicts.source: https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/concepts/policies; WebSearch ran query "HashiCorp Vault KV secrets branching per-user secret paths identity templating"
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a negative claim about a competitor. Vault supports per-user KV paths through identity-templated policies, so "does not support personal configs" may be overstated depending on how ESC defines "personal configs".

verdicts.text: The `pulumi env diff` command shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC CLI source for `env diff` has the help text: "This command displays the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment." `pulumi env` uses the same ESC env command set.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault does not support comparing secrets across environments.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Third-party comparisons agree that Vault has no built-in way to compare secrets across environments. Doppler says "Vault also does not provide a visual diffing mechanism for comparing application secrets between environments". Infisical says Vault has "no native concept of environments", so users simulate them with paths and compare values by hand. Both sources are competitors, and I found no official HashiCorp page that settles this negative claim.
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is an absolute negative claim, and the evidence comes only from competitors. Vault KV v2 does offer version history within a single path, and scripted CLI diffs across paths are possible, so "does not support" is really about native or UI support.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports built-in functions such as `toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `fromBase64`, and `toString` that allow data manipulation for any scenario.
verdicts.evidence: pulumi/esc ast/expr.go says objects whose single key names a builtin function are parsed as a BuiltinExpr through tryParseFunction. My output was cut off before the list of function names, so I could not confirm fn::toJSON, fn::fromJSON, fn::fromBase64 and fn::toString in fetched source. They match the ESC builtins I know of, but I have not confirmed that in this session. "For any scenario" is marketing overstatement and can't be checked.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "allow data manipulation for any scenario" overstates; ESC offers a fixed small set of builtins (join/split/toJSON/fromJSON/toBase64/fromBase64/toString/secret/open/rotate).

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault provides templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine, rather than functions for composing configuration values.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs confirm that both features exist. Username templating is "used in some secret engines to allow operators to define how dynamic usernames are generated", and the Transform secrets engine has its own docs and API pages (transformations, templates, alphabets). The "rather than functions for composing configuration values" part is a characterization that these docs don't directly address.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault Agent templating (Consul Template) and VSO secret transformation render secrets into config files, so "rather than functions for composing configuration values" may understate Vault's ecosystem. Also, Transform is an Enterprise-only (ADP) feature.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault supports audit logs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's official Vault docs: "Audit devices are mountable devices that log requests and responses in Vault." They note auditing is off by default on new clusters and you have to turn it on.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC uses TLS for encryption in transit and unique encryption keys per environment for encryption at rest.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) I couldn't find a public source saying ESC uses per-environment encryption keys. The Pulumi IaC FAQ only states the per-stack rule: "For every stack Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key." The ESC environments docs only say fn::secret values are "encrypted at rest," and neither page mentions TLS for ESC.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "Pulumi ESC encryption at rest per environment key TLS in transit" and "Pulumi ESC FAQ \"unique encryption key\" environment"; top results only covered per-stack keys for IaC (pulumi.com/docs/iac/faq, pulumi.com/docs/esc/concepts/environments/)
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Unique key per environment" looks like it was carried over from the documented per-stack key rule for IaC. Check it against ESC product source (pulumi/esc, ESC FAQ) before publishing.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend, which automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit AES cipher in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Security Model page says: "Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend. The security barrier automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher in the Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces." Vault's source (barrier_aes_gcm.go) matches this: a 256-bit key and a 12-byte nonce.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim almost exactly restates the HashiCorp security model docs. The only change is shortening "Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)" to "AES".

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault supports access controls.
verdicts.evidence: Vault's access control is built on ACL policies, and the Pulumi Vault provider exposes a `vault.Policy` resource for managing them (sdk/nodejs/policy.ts is in pulumi/pulumi-vault). I didn't check this against HashiCorp's own docs, but the claim is basic and widely documented.

verdicts.text: HashiCorp Vault's cloud secrets engines generate short-lived credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, with each engine configured with a static credential that Vault uses to mint them.
verdicts.evidence: The first half holds: Vault's AWS, Azure and GCP secrets engines do mint dynamic, short-lived credentials. But the claim that every engine is configured with a static credential is out of date. HashiCorp says these plugins "originally required static security credentials." Plugin WIF gives "secretless configuration for the AWS, GCP, and Azure secrets engines," available from Vault Enterprise 1.16/1.17.
verdicts.framing_note: The static-credential setup is the traditional/Community Edition default, but it is not universal. Rewording to "typically configured with" or "by default configured with," or mentioning Enterprise WIF, would make it accurate.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Each engine configured with a static credential" is written as an absolute. It leaves out Enterprise WIF and ambient credentials (instance metadata / managed identity).

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the Pulumi SDK, CLI, UI, and `pulumi-service` provider.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi-service provider does ship an OIDC resource (examples/cs-oidc-issuer). But that resource registers external OIDC issuers that Pulumi Cloud trusts. It doesn't make Pulumi Cloud act as an OIDC provider. I found nothing in the repo or source that backs the claim that Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the SDK, CLI, UI, and provider. The sibling comparison pages (doppler.md, infisical.md) don't make this claim either; their row is "OIDC Trust: trust relationships are established with third-party OIDC providers".
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/pulumi-pulumiservice/contents/examples; repo:content/docs/esc/vs/doppler.md L148-150; repo:content/docs/esc/vs/infisical.md L148-150
verdicts.intuition_flag: The claim may mix up two things: Pulumi Cloud issuing OIDC tokens to AWS, Azure, and GCP, and Pulumi Cloud trusting outside OIDC issuers (the OidcIssuer resource). It's also unclear what "used as an OIDC provider from the CLI" would mean.

verdicts.text: Configuring HashiCorp Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
verdicts.evidence: The Pulumi Vault provider ships a `vault.identity.OidcProvider` resource, documented as "Manages OIDC Providers in a Vault server", and it links to Vault's HTTP API docs for oidc-provider. So you can configure Vault as an OIDC provider through infrastructure as code and the HTTP API, not only the CLI. Vault's UI probably supports it too, but I didn't check that in this session.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim is also inconsistent with the same page's own row (L86), which says Vault resources can be managed with the Vault provider for Pulumi or Terraform.
